protagonist: Marcus Ibe, junior estimator, Solvane Tile & Stone

deliverables.text: An interior-angle-sum tessellation proof for both patterns: compute the regular hexagon's interior angle and show 3 meeting at a vertex sum to 360 degrees; compute the regular octagon's interior angle and show 3 alone do not sum to 360 degrees but 2 octagons + 1 square do.

A staging-block computation using the greatest common factor of the plaza's stated length and width, giving the largest evenly-dividing square staging block and how many blocks are needed per dimension.

A cut-waste computation for both tiling options: sheets purchased (rounding up every partial row/column) against the plaza's dimensions, plus the standard installation waste allowance, expressed as a waste percentage of tile purchased.
A total installed cost table: material cost and labor cost (including any pattern-specific labor premium) for each option, and the resulting total installed cost per square foot.

A recommendation memo defended with D1's geometry, D3's waste percentages, and D4's total installed cost per square foot, including how close the two options come and whether that margin is comfortable enough to bid with confidence.

appendices.title: Option A — The Regular Hexagon Pattern
Option B — The Octagon-and-Square Combination Pattern

balance.argument_a: The Regular Hexagon Pattern's single-shape geometry tessellates the plane with zero gaps (D1) and needs no pattern-specific labor coordination beyond one repeating shape. Its total installed cost, $17.71/sq ft, is real and computed from the listed price of a real manufactured tile line (S1), a real waste-allowance figure (S3), and a real published labor-cost range (S4) -- and it wins even though its listed tile price per square foot is 32% below Option B's, meaning the cost advantage survives once cut-waste and a mosaic labor premium are both counted against it.
balance.argument_b: The Octagon-and-Square Combination Pattern's manufactured sheet is a perfect 12x12in (1 sq ft) square (S2) that divides the plaza's whole-foot dimensions with zero grid-rounding waste, giving it the lower of the two waste percentages (9.1% vs. Option A's 10.5%, Appendix E) and no labor premium (its clean square-grid repeat needs no pattern-specific labor adjustment, Appendix F). It is the client's stated design preference, and the margin between the two options is real but modest -- 9.9%, not a rout.
balance.margin_basis: Compute each option's total installed cost per square foot of the 1,350 sq ft plaza (material cost from purchased sheet coverage x listed price per sq ft, plus labor cost from plaza area x labor rate including any pattern premium), then compare the two totals.
balance.margin_note: COMPUTED 2026-09-01 (case-research). Option A (Hexagon): sheet grid 47x36=1,692 positions (bounding rectangle 11.625in x 10.25in = 0.96875ft x 0.854167ft against the 45ft x 30ft plaza); + Appendix E's 10% install waste allowance -> 1,862 sheets purchased (1,692 x 1.10 = 1,861.2, rounded up); purchased coverage = 1,862 x 0.81 sq ft/sheet (S1) = 1,508.22 sq ft; material cost = 1,508.22 x $6.59 (S1) = $9,939.17. Labor: base rate $9.00/sq ft (MA3) x 1.15 hexagon premium (MA4) = $10.35/sq ft x 1,350 sq ft = $13,972.50. Total A = $9,939.17 + $13,972.50 = $23,911.67 -> $23,911.67 / 1,350 = $17.71/sq ft. Option B (Octagon+Square): sheet grid 45x30=1,350 positions (12in x 12in = 1ft x 1ft sheet divides the 45ft x 30ft plaza exactly, zero remainder); + 10% waste allowance -> 1,485 sheets purchased (1,350 x 1.10 = 1,485.0 exactly); purchased coverage = 1,485 x 1.00 sq ft/sheet (S2) = 1,485 sq ft; material cost = 1,485 x $9.69 (S2) = $14,389.65. Labor: base rate $9.00/sq ft (MA3), no premium (Appendix F) x 1,350 sq ft = $12,150.00. Total B = $14,389.65 + $12,150.00 = $26,539.65 -> $26,539.65 / 1,350 = $19.66/sq ft. margin_pct = (19.66 - 17.71) / 19.66 x 100 = 1.95 / 19.66 x 100 = 9.92%, rounded to 9.9%. WINNER: Option A, The Regular Hexagon Pattern. This is well inside SPEC Section 2's ~20% cap -- no retune needed. Full arithmetic also reproduced in sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Stated scenario dimensions -- Ashford's plaza is fictional, so no real blueprint exists to cite. Chosen for a clean, computable GCF (15) for Appendix B.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- every downstream computation (Appendices B, E, F) depends on these exact dimensions.

modeling_assumptions.claim: Days from case launch to bid deadline
modeling_assumptions.basis: Narrative flavor, matching the Overview's same-week urgency.
Midpoint of the real published $3-$15/sq ft range (S4). No more specific published rate exists for this fictional job.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: MEDIUM -- scales both options' labor cost proportionally; Option A's labor is always 15% higher than Option B's at any base rate, but margin_pct does shift with this choice (see sensitivity_model.py).

modeling_assumptions.claim: Labor premium for Option A (hexagon mosaic installation)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single published percentage exists for a hexagon-vs-square-grid mosaic labor premium; S4/S5/S6 confirm mosaic/small-format tile takes measurably longer to install, but only qualitatively. 15% is a round, moderate value inside that general direction.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- the single most decision-relevant modeling choice in the case. At 0% premium, Option A's margin widens to ~16.8%. Near a ~37% premium (more than double the 15% used), the winner flips to Option B. See sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.claim: Cut-waste computed via each sheet's bounding-rectangle grid fit, not the true offset/staggered hexagon-row pattern within a sheet
modeling_assumptions.basis: A full staggered-hex-offset cutting model is beyond MS-level geometry; the bounding-rectangle grid method is the same simplification real estimators use for a first-pass material takeoff.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: MEDIUM -- a more precise staggered-offset model would likely lower Option A's computed waste slightly, which would strengthen (not weaken) Option A's case -- so this simplification is conservative in the direction of understating Option A's advantage.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (9.9%) is real but modest, and the case's single most decision-relevant lever is MA4 (the hexagon labor premium), not a sourced figure. At MA4=0%, Option A's margin widens to ~16.8%; near MA4=37% (more than double the 15% value used), the winner flips to Option B. MA3 (base labor rate) scales both options' labor cost but does not by itself flip the winner at any of the published range's endpoints ($3-$15/sq ft), since it does not change the 15% relative gap between the two labor rates. See sensitivity_model.py for the full sweep and case.json's balance.margin_note for the base-case arithmetic trail.

cohort_bands.note: The size the case was authored for. Socratic plan and Anchor timings run as written (45 minutes, all 4 anchors, full twist, threaded deep conflict).

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; the twist still drops at the same relative point but only one deep-conflict thread runs (recommend thread 1, 'the tessellation math and the real cut-waste math point in opposite directions,' since it has the sharpest conceptual payoff); total runtime shortens to roughly 30 minutes, content held constant.

No vote to take at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position instead. The facilitator plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands; 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse your bid recommendation, and why.'
